title: Scrambled Eggs
subtitle: Soft, slow-cooked scrambled eggs on buttered toast
excerpt: Eggs beaten with a little milk, cooked gently over low heat in a generous amount of butter, stirred constantly until just set and still slightly glossy. The slowness is the technique.

recipe.sourceNotes: Properly soft scrambled eggs are cooked very slowly over low heat with a generous amount of butter, stirred constantly, and removed from the heat while still slightly underdone. The residual heat in the pan finishes the cooking. The method is associated with British chef Heston Blumenthal and French classical technique. The common mistake is too much heat, which produces rubbery, watery scrambled eggs that overcook before leaving the pan.

recipeTools.notes: A small, heavy-based saucepan or non-stick pan.

content.text: Keep the heat low throughout. If the pan feels too hot, lift it off the heat and continue stirring. Remove the eggs from the heat when they are still slightly under-done: they will continue to cook in the pan for another 30 seconds. Overcooked scrambled eggs are dry and rubbery; properly soft ones are creamy and glossy.
Beat the eggs with the milk and a pinch of salt in a bowl until combined but not frothy.

Melt the butter in a small, heavy-based saucepan over very low heat. Pour in the egg mixture. Cook, stirring constantly with a rubber spatula, for 4 to 6 minutes. Keep moving the spatula across the base of the pan in slow, deliberate strokes.

Remove from the heat when the eggs are softly set but still slightly glossy and wet-looking. The residual heat will finish them. Season with salt and pepper. Serve immediately on buttered toast, scattered with chives.
